#4922. The 9 Most Walkable Cities in the US

Anyone who’s been to the pump lately could appreciate a little less reliance on cars. And while life in the most walkable cities in the US can mean saving on gas (not to mention car insurance, parking, and potential parking tickets), getting around on foot isn’t only about your budget. Walkability “can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” says Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, which has been following and analyzing walkability for years with their Walk Score tool. “There’s also a housing-market component: People tend to value the convenience and access that comes with living in a walkable neighborhood, and that desirability can translate into high home values. Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors,” says Fairweather.

To determine the country’s most walkable cities, we’ve reviewed recent studies, like the one from Only in Your State, a travel and discovery platform, plus talked to realtors, residents, and tourism experts across the country.

Hoboken is located on the banks of the Hudson River.

Just across the Hudson River from Manhattan, Hoboken is the most walkable city in the US, according to Only in Your State’s most recent analysis. The one-square-mile-city earned a nearly perfect Walk Score of 97, thanks to its dense street grid, many mixed-use buildings, and abundance of public transportation. Three other cities in the Garden State also cracked the list’s top 10: Union City, West New York, and Jersey City.

Though LA isn’t known for being particularly pedestrian friendly, West Hollywood remains a walkable enclave.

Los Angeles County isn’t known for its public transit, but even so, West Hollywood snagged the fourth spot in Only in Your State’s analysis, earning a Walk Score of 91. The city packs over 300 restaurants, bars, and coffee shops into just under two square miles. West Hollywood’s walkability is especially prized because the area is one of LA’s most vibrant nightlife districts, creating safe accessibility for revelers on the world-famous Sunset Strip.

In addition to being one of the country’s oldest, Boston is also one of the most walkable cities.

“What makes Boston special is that every neighborhood has its own personality and you can experience so much of the city on foot,” says George Sarkis, CEO and cofounder of the Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman. “You can walk from the historic brownstones of Beacon Hill to the boutiques and restaurants of Back Bay, through the Public Garden, and into the South End without ever feeling like you’re covering much ground.” Walking is the best way to truly enjoy all of the city’s historic sites, centuries-old architecture, and cobblestone streets.

San Francisco’s hilly landscape can turn a casual stroll into an all-in workout.

This Bay Area city has one of the highest transit scores in the country, making it a breeze to go car-free. But for many locals—like Wendy Newman, a realtor with Wesely & Associates and a resident since 1987—walking is the real experience. “​​In one outing, you can buy groceries, stop for coffee, admire a Victorian’s unreasonable paint palette, nod at the neighbor whose face you know but whose name you still haven’t learned, and discover a bookstore you weren’t looking for,” she says. Plus, San Francisco’s mild climate makes taking a spin through neighborhoods like Chinatown and North Beach enjoyable year round.

New York City is built on a grid system, making it easy to navigate.

Just about every expert we talked to mentioned NYC, a metropolis made for a good stroll. From the café-lined lanes of Little Italy to particularly scenic stretches like the East River Promenade and Brooklyn Bridge Park, the Big Apple is big on pedestrian access. And the city’s high walkability score has benefits beyond just saving on cab fare, points out Kate Wollman-Mahan, a real estate agent at Christie’s International Real Estate New York. “Life expectancy in New York City is five years longer than the national average, according to the city-run Health Dashboard and economist Jonathan Miller (82.3 years versus 77.3 years),” she says. “Walking is built into everyday life, from going out to coffee to running errands to walking in the park.”

A stroll around DC can take pedestrians past national monuments and charming townhouses.

According to Walk Score, a research platform that promotes walkability, DC has a walk score of 98. It's such a popular pedestrian playground that even local cultural institutions embed walking into their education approach. Take the Spy Museum, for example, which developed its own free walking tour because of the breadth of strolling space in the area and interest from both residents and tourists. “We send them around the National Mall and downtown area with espionage history that happened in those exact places throughout history,” says Aliza Bran, the museum’s director of media relations. Other particularly walkable neighborhoods include Dupont Circle, U Street, Capitol Hill, and Georgetown.

The Windy City is a certified walking city.

The Windy City tops the US ranking for walkability from Preply, a language learning marketplace that runs walkability studies across the US, Europe, and Asia. “You can walk between Chicago’s five most-visited attractions (the Art Institute, Millennium Park, Cloud Gate, the Chicago Architecture Center, and the Magnificent Mile) in 28 minutes, about 2,500 steps,” says Preply’s communications leader Madeline Enos.

Sheldon Bishop, the founder of BrewAtlas, a guide to independent specialty coffee shops, argues that the best sign of a walkable neighborhood is a good cafe. And Chicago is particularly well caffeinated, thanks to 95 specialty cafes across 41 neighborhoods. “When people can walk to get coffee, they run into neighbors, stop into the bookstore next door, and spend money on the block instead of at a drive-thru,” he says.

Miami is full of walkable pockets, according to local residents.

For Sandra Masis, director of sales at the residential building Arbor Coconut Grove, it’s neighborhoods like Coconut Grove that make Miami such a pedestrian-friendly city. “You can walk to restaurants, cafés, shops, parks, and the waterfront, all while enjoying the neighborhood’s lush greenery and relaxed atmosphere,” she says. “It has a sense of community that makes you want to get outside and explore.” And Miami’s newer developments, like Brickell, prioritize walkability as much as older neighborhoods like Coconut Grove and Little Havana. “Even in a city built around cars, you can create pockets where people can comfortably live, work, and socialize on foot,” says Masis.

Contemporary high-rises mingle with historic sites in Philadelphia.

Every year GuruWalk, a platform for free tours, puts together a ranking of the best cities in the world to explore on foot. In their most recent study, NYC took the top spot among US cities, and Philadelphia came in just behind it. GuruWalk’s Carolina Martínez says that though Philly gets fewer visitors than other places on the list, those who explore it love it. “Philadelphia has a 4.99 average rating, with 99 percent of reviews at five stars,” she says. “Walk a few blocks through the historic district and you’re standing in front of Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell.” New Orleans, San Francisco, and Boston round out the top five.

#4920. Listen, I Think Josh O’Connor Should Be James Bond

The Challengers star would bring a new energy—and a new brand of modern masculinity—to the world’s most famous spy.

WHEN THE NAMES of the rumored final contenders to play the next James Bond were floated in the press a couple of weeks ago—seemingly Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and a mystery third candidate, according to Deadline—I heard a lot of the same sentiment afterward. In more or less words, a lot of people seemed to say “I love Josh O’Connor, but he shouldn’t be Bond.” When I dropped the link into a group chat full of people who aren’t inhaling movie news like I am, there was another probably common response: “I don’t know who that guy is, but he doesn’t look like Bond.”

To me, that sentiment is exactly why O’Connor is the best—and, in some ways, the only—choice to be the next James Bond.

For those not familiar, O’Connor, a 36-year-old Brit who grew up in Cheltenham, has been a working actor for more than a decade, but his star has only really begun to shine in the 2020s. He won an Emmy for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and more recently has made splashes in movies like the thrilling and sexy sports film Challengers, Rian Johnson’s third Knives Out film Wake Up Dead Man (which, ironically, he appeared in alongside previous Bond Daniel Craig), and this summer’s Steven Spielberg blockbuster Disclosure Day.

It’s not hard to understand why some people’s minds might naturally push against the idea of O’Connor as Bond. Where 007 is typically a classically handsome, devilishly smooth gentleman who almost looks like a video game simulation—seriously, look back at Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan for just a second—O’Connor is a bit off-kilter. His hair is wavy; his ears are prominent; his smile is asymmetrical. There’s no beating around the bush—he’s been compared more often to Linguini from Pixar’s Ratatouille than the idea most people have of what a James Bond should be.

But it’s through those eccentricities that O’Connor shines. If you take the time to watch his performances, you’ll find the constant image of someone who brings an undeniable charisma to every project, and somehow manages to mold that into something different each time. In Challengers, O’Connor is the kind of guy you want to root against—he’s sleazy, not a particularly good friend, and unrefined. But he brings the perfect bit of steamy, compelling energy to a love triangle that wouldn’t be the same without him. Co-stars Mike Faist and Zendaya are deserving of credit (as are composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross), but O’Connor’s charm is what makes the whole movie work.

He pulls a similar magic trick with just about every other performance. In Wake Up Dead Man, he plays a former boxer-turned-priest who once accidentally killed a man in the ring. Throughout the course of the film, O’Connor goes from someone who wrestles with guilt, shame, and intrigue to someone who can believably talk someone struggling with grief off a ledge—all while both trying to solve a murder and possibly being suspected of that same murder at the same time. In Kelly Reichardt’s The Mastermind, O’Connor plays a less-than-competent, hardly aspirational art thief who stumbles his way through charged political times. Despite this, O’Connor is so magnetic on screen that it’s just about impossible not to like him.

But it’s not just the way he elevates sleazeballs and losers into undeniably watchable men (although that doesn’t hurt). O’Connor has shown a propensity to play traditionally enchanting as well. In La Chimera, from Italian filmmaker Alice Rohrwacher, he’s cool, sleek, and morally gray in a movie that may be the blueprint for what his Bond could potentially look like. He’s got a likable way about him that’s different from some of the manly men (like Connery), sleek operators (like Brosnan), or rugged action stars (like Craig) who’ve played the role before; His charm is distinctly more modern, oozing from nothing other than being a guy who knows how to talk to people, and do it really well.

O’Connor’s quirks and oddities, may, at first glance, be what seems to make him an unfit choice to play Bond. But the key is to look at O’Connor’s unique look and gifts as a feature rather than a bug. People might say Bond needs to look this way, and sound that way, and otherwise it doesn’t work. But for anyone who feels so strongly about that, there’s good news: There are 25 other canonical James Bond movies (plus 1967’s Casino Royale and 1983’s Never Say Never Again) where he almost always looks and behaves just like that. When better than now to try something new? Daniel Craig’s blond hair and untraditional look were also questioned at first, and it’s safe to say that risk turned out pretty well in the end.

The forthcoming Bond movie has Denis Villeneuve signed on as director, and Villeneuve has pretty much never failed when it comes to casting his movies. Can you imagine anyone other than Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides in his Dune movies? It seems like an obvious pick now, but the 30-year-old Oscar nominee had only just begun to break out when he was cast in the role back in 2018. Villeneuve has a clear eye for talent, and so it won’t be much of a stretch to trust in whoever ultimately lands the job—but it’s hard to not be excited about a director of his caliber linking up with an actor as ambitious and high-reaching as O’Connor.

Plus, it’s worth noting that the Bond franchise isn’t quite like other mega-series out there. Since the Craig era began with 2006’s Casino Royale, Bond movies have come out on average every three or four years. That’s spread out enough for O’Connor to continue taking on fun, exciting projects even outside of the role as everyone’s favorite super spy.

The other choices aren’t bad. Callum Turner gets a bad rap after his appearance in One Night Only, but he’s shown promise in projects like Green Room and Masters of the Air, and Apple TV’s new Neuromancer looks good. Jack Lowden has played one of television’s most beloved spies for six seasons on Slow Horses—the fit would be seamless. Whoever Villeneuve picks (even if it’s the unnamed mystery actor) will be afforded a huge amount of goodwill.

But isn’t the fact that O’Connor elicits such a reaction—consistently in his on-screen roles and through the mere idea of him becoming James Bond—proof that he’s the right pick?

#4918. Inside the Governor’s Mansions That Will Soon Be Home to 19 Newly Elected Leaders

In January, the United States’ 19 newly elected governors won’t just have inauguration day on their calendars, but moving day, too. All but five states have governor’s mansions for their leaders to live and work from, with the exceptions being Arizona, Idaho, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont. These executive residences tend to be grand in style and scale, often possessing a long, rich history—even some haunted ones.

Sometimes, governors forego their official residences in favor of privately owned homes. For example, California governor Gavin Newsom recently listed the $7.5 million Fair Oaks home he lived in instead of the official executive residence, a 19th-century Victorian in Sacramento. Montana’s governor’s mansion is currently empty and in disrepair, while a governor hasn’t inhabited the official residence in Nebraska in over a decade.

Most states, however, have longstanding traditions of their leaders living in their official governor’s mansions. Virginia has the oldest continuously inhabited executive residence—every governor has lived there since 1813. If our new league of governors opts for tradition, here’s where they will be resting their heads for the next few years.

Republican Tommy Tuberville won Alabama’s gubernatorial race and will be able to move into a 119-year-old mansion in Montgomery following his inauguration. Built in 1907 by architect T. Weatherly Carter, the 17-room neoclassical residence features a row of four Corinthian columns at its front entrance, which opens to a foyer with a grand bifurcated staircase.

California’s new governor-elect is democrat Xavier Becerra, who will soon reside at a three-story Victorian in Sacramento. Built in 1877, the 20,000-square-foot house was thoroughly renovated in 2015, decades after Ronald and Nancy Reagan’s brief stint living there in 1967 before deeming it uninhabitable. The mansion was then used as a museum until its 2015 update, when it became home to the state’s governors once again. It has 30 rooms, Italian marble fireplaces, original wood floors, and a kidney-shaped swimming pool.

In Denver, democrat Phil Weiser will receive the keys to the red brick governor’s mansion known as Colorado’s Home. Built in 1908, it has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1960. The Colonial Revival–style home has 27 rooms and shares its one-acre grounds with gardens, a historic gazebo, a greenhouse, and a carriage house. Thanks to John Hickenlooper, governor from 2011 to 2019, the home also has a rotating selection of local beers on tap.

Republican Byron Donalds just made history as Florida’s first Black governor. The state’s Greek Revival–style governor’s mansion in Tallahassee was completed in 1956 on the site of the original governor’s mansion built in 1907, which had fallen into disrepair. A screened swimming pool, a greenhouse, and a rose garden are among its amenities.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has the distinction of being the first Black woman governor-elect in the United States. Her soon-to-be residence in Atlanta is a 30-room Greek Revival mansion that was built in 1967 by architect A. Thomas Bradbury. Across three levels, it measures in at 30,000 square feet.

Iowa’s governor’s mansion, known as Terrace Hill, will soon be home to democrat Rob Sand. Dating all the way back to 1869, Terrace Hill is an 18,000-square-foot Second Empire–style residence in Des Moines where Iowa’s governors have lived since 1976. Its first two floors are open to the public as a museum and events space.

Democrat Hannah Pingree will move into the Blaine House in Augusta, Maine. Originally built in 1833 in a combination of Federal and Greek Revival styles, the mansion has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1919, when renovations gave it a more Colonial style. It has 28 rooms across two stories, including a billiards room. The property also hosts a formal garden and a tennis court.

In Michigan, democrat Jocelyn Benson has the good fortune of governing a state with two official executive residences: one in the state’s capital of Lansing, and an official summer residence on Mackinac Island. The former is a 1957-built 8,700-square-foot ranch-style home with five bedrooms and four bathrooms; the latter is an Arts-and-Crafts-style mansion that was built in 1901.

Democrat Amy Klobuchar, currently a US senator for Minnesota, won her state’s gubernatorial election and will move into a 16,000-square-foot residence in St. Paul that dates to 1912. It features seven bedrooms, 10 bathrooms, and nine fireplaces. Architect William Channing Whitney designed the stone-and-brick dwelling in a combination of English Tudor and Beaux-Arts styles.

Nevada also elected its first Black governor, democrat Aaron Ford, who will soon reside in a Classical Revival–style mansion designed by architect George A. Ferris in 1909. It features a grand entrance hall, a reception room, a formal dining room, a governor’s study, and a luncheon room, in addition to private living quarters.

New Mexico’s governor-elect, democrat Deb Haaland, has made history as the first Native American woman to hold that title. In Santa Fe, the governor’s mansion is referred to as The People’s House. Designed by architect W.C. Kruger, the midcentury-modern structure was completed in 1955.

Democrat Amy Acton will be Ohio’s next governor, granting her residency inside a 1925 mansion in Bexley, just outside of Columbus. The Tudor-style home was built by architect Robert Gilmore Hanford, and its grounds boast three acres of extensive gardens, including a “Storybook Trail” inspired by The Tales of Peter Rabbit.

Republican governor-elect Mike Mazzei will be the new steward of Oklahoma’s official governor’s residence in Tulsa. The 14,000-square-foot Dutch Colonial was built in 1928 and has a limestone façade that matches the State Capitol building two blocks away. Uniquely, its grounds boast a swimming pool shaped like Oklahoma, an outdoor kitchen, and a tennis court on the former site of a helipad where President Lyndon B. Johnson landed in 1964.

Helena Foulkes, a democrat, won the race for Rhode Island’s governor, but she isn’t necessarily going to move out of her current residence any time soon, since the state doesn’t have an official governor’s mansion. Foulkes owns two homes in the state: a $3.8 million eight-bedroom summer house in Narragansett and a $2.3 million three-bedroom home in Providence.

Republican governor-elect Alan Wilson won South Carolina’s vote, making his next home a two-story Federal-style mansion dating back to 1855. Originally used as military academy officers’ quarters, it has been the official governor’s residence since 1868, three years after the Civil War ended. Inside, it has a central entrance hall connecting to two drawing rooms, a state dining room, and a library. Private living quarters are located on the second floor.

Marsha Blackburn, the Republican governor-elect of Tennessee, can move to a 10-acre estate in Nashville’s Oak Hill suburb. Known as Far Hills for the surrounding picturesque views, the three-story Georgian-style mansion was built in 1931. It has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1949.

In Texas, democrat Gina Hinojosa will be the first Latina to hold the state’s highest office. Her official residence will be a Greek Revival–style mansion in Austin. Spanning nearly 10,000 square feet, it has been home to Texas’s governors since it was built in 1856.

Democrat David Crowley won in Wisconsin, making him the first Black governor of the state. The state’s executive residence is a Classical Revival–style mansion located in Madison. Completed in 1928, it has 16,000 square feet of interior living space across three floors, including seven bedrooms, 13 bathrooms, seven fireplaces, and 10 gardens.

Republican Eric Barlow will soon have access to the governor’s residence near Frontier Park in Cheyenne, Wyoming. In 1976, it replaced the state’s former executive residence, which was built in 1905 and is now open as a museum. Available details of the current mansion are sparse, however, and it seems that a new, upgraded version with improved security and functionality may soon be in the works.

#4917. The Best Foot Baths for Soothing Tired Feet, According to Podiatrists

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes. But since I don’t have the time or endless funds to regularly hoof it to my local spa for a foot massage or pedicure, a home foot bath is my go-to. The best foot baths allow you to soak your tired toes, with extra features like bubbles, jets, and massage functions to help your feet feel rejuvenated.

A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health. But unsurprisingly, a lot of the potential perks from home foot baths revolve around your feet. These baths can help boost circulation in your feet and combat inflammation that could lead to pain, swelling, and overuse injuries if it’s left unchecked, says Bradley Schaeffer, DPM, a podiatrist and foot surgeon specializing in sports medicine in New York City. Plus, now that we’re at peak cozy season, shopping for a great foot bath for yourself or a loved one (it’s a great gift for her!) is a cost-effective way to give your feet some R&R.

Doing foot baths a few times a week can help to slough off dead skin that builds up quickly, leaving you with softer, less grody-looking feet, says Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois

Not all foot baths are created equal, and it’s important to choose one based on your needs. So, if bubbles make you feel uncomfortable (me, hi), a foot bath that simply swirls around warm water may be more your speed. We also tapped Schaeffer, Lockwood, and Suzanne C. Fuchs, DPM, a podiatrist at Luxe Podiatry in Jupiter, Florida, for their advice on what to look for when shopping for these foot health-supportive devices and to get their feedback on their favorites.

Using that guidance and our personal experience, we found factors like size, weight, and additional features matter when choosing a foot bath. At baseline, a foot bath is a container to hold water to soothe your feet. But there are plenty of specific features to keep in mind when shopping for a foot bath.

The Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa packs a lot of features into a device you can fold flat. A huge highlight is the eight groups of massaging balls that go to work to ease pressure on the bottoms of your feet. (These aren’t motorized, but you can run your feet over them for a soothing effect.) While it’s a good idea to start out with warm or hot water, the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa has temperature adjustment, allowing you to ramp up the heat between 95 and 118 degrees Fahrenheit without having to toss in more liquid. An LED display keeps tabs on the water temperature, giving you real-time information on how hot it is.

As the name suggests, this foot bath is collapsible and drops down when it’s not in use, making it easy to slide into or under tight spaces. A few potential downsides to consider: Hospan’s bubbles aren’t the strongest you’ll find, and this is a pricier bath when it’s not on sale, although it’s usually marked down a few times a year. But if you’re looking to pamper your feet with a range of options and are okay with investing a little extra, this is a solid choice that will hold up well and does just about everything.

It’s hard to find a foot bath that checks all the boxes, but the Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath comes really close. This bath allows you to get a good soak with a few extras to take your experience to a new level. “This model features massage settings, which can enhance relaxation,” Fuchs says.

This bath has a modest price tag of $30, which is significantly less than some others you’ll come across. It also uses vibration for a massage and has a pinpoint massage tool in the center in case you want to work on a particular area of your foot. While there’s no bubble feature, not everyone is into bubbles (they tickle my feet, which isn’t my favorite).

Conair’s foot bath is easy to use and clean, and offers plenty of opportunities to pamper your feet. The Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath uses a toe-touch control to turn the vibration settings on and off, although there’s no remote. This bath isn’t powerful enough to heat up cool or room temperature water, but it does a solid job of keeping already-warm liquid at the same temperature.

Not every foot bath has a bubble feature, and some are stronger than others. If bubbles are a priority for you, Fuchs recommends the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath. “Known for its bubbling action, this foot spa provides a soothing experience,” she says.

The bath delivers plenty of bubbles, along with heat, to create a spa-like feel while you soak. It also has three pedicure attachments that pop into the center: a massager, brush, and pumice stone. Those attachments neatly fit into on-board storage when they’re not being used. An ergonomic footbed with massaging bristles on the bottom of the bath also helps cushion your soles while you rest. The whole thing folds up pretty small, and has a special locking system for when it’s filled up.

If you’re interested in a foot bath that will give you a shiatsu-type massage, this isn’t it. But if you love the idea of blissfully scrolling on your phone while your feet are surrounded by warm, bubbly goodness, the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath is the right choice.

Getting the temperature just right in your foot bath can be tricky. But the Sharper Image Spa Haven Foot Bath has temperature control, allowing you to punch in the level of heat you want up to 108 degrees and let it go to work for you. This foot bath is loaded with features, including separate bubble and heat options, and free-spinning massaging rollers on the bottom that allow you to control the pressure and speed. (The rollers are removable for cleaning.)

The bubbling action is delivered in your choice of four speeds, and there’s also a removable pumice stone to help get rid of calluses and dead skin. When you’re done with your foot bath, just open the drain plug to let the water seep out. The only major downside to this foot bath (besides the high price) is that it’s not collapsible. But that also means it’s sturdy enough to rest your feet on the side when you want to take a break—a feature you won’t find in baths that break down.

The Medical King Foot Spa has six sets of massaging rollers to help knead out stress and pain after a long day. Couple that with bubble jets, vibration settings, and a built-in heater, and you’ve got a recipe for a good time.

This relatively affordable foot bath comes with a remote control that doubles as a control panel, with clear buttons to adjust the massage mode and flip through three temperature settings as you kick back. You can also set a timer to cut off the features whenever you want. The foot bath is collapsible, so storage under your bed or couch shouldn’t be an issue. This foot bath delivers if you’re looking for a way to work out kinks in your soles without having to put in any major effort.

You can splash out on a bunch of different features when it comes to a foot bath, but sometimes you just want a standard soak. If that’s the case—and you want to save some cash, too—consider the Mantello Foot Bath. This barebones bath is as basic as they come, but it has a few features that elevate it above your standard plastic bucket.

The bath has a sturdy plastic design that won’t tip over easily. It’s also deep, giving you plenty of space to soak your calves, too. The base has built-in arch support and raised dots for a little something extra while your feet relax. The open design means it’s easy to clean, too. There are no bubbles, massagers, or built-in heaters. But for a mere $23, what do you expect? If you’re just looking to unwind with a solid soak, this is a great choice.

“Foot baths can offer several benefits for foot health,” Fuchs says. She lists off a bunch of potential perks, including helping your muscles (and mind) relax, improved circulation, removing the buildup of dirt and bacteria, soothing conditions like athlete’s foot or plantar fasciitis, and exfoliation. Of course, you don’t have to use a foot bath to have good foot health—but many people find that it can be a comfortable way to support it.

Should you use Epsom salts in your foot bath?

In case you’re not familiar with them, Epsom salts can help soften skin and support muscle relaxation. Fuchs recommends adding Epsom salts or essential oils to your tub to ramp up the relaxation and health perks.

The odds are good that you’ll be hauling a foot bath in and out of a storage spot on a regular basis. Most foot baths aren’t overly heavy, but some higher-tech options have more heft to them than others. (The baths we recommend range from 1 pound to 9 pounds.) Just take a peek at the weight to make sure you can comfortably carry your device around.

If your feet are on the larger side, you want to make sure there’s enough room for them to fit comfortably inside your bath. Also, that foot bath has to go somewhere, both when it’s put away and in use. Check the dimensions and compare them to where you plan to use your bath, along with the drawer or closet space where you plan to stash it, to make sure you have enough room.

This came up with every podiatrist we spoke to. “Feet can get gross and we want to be able to have a sanitized bath each time we use it,” Lockwood says. Schaeffer agrees. “Bacteria can grow in these, raising the risk of infections,” he points out. With that, it’s crucial to look for a foot bath that’s easy to clean. That usually means the bath can be disassembled for scrub-downs or at least have very detailed cleaning instructions.

This isn’t a requirement, but having the option to collapse your foot bath can be helpful if you’re short on storage space. Many collapsible foot baths can fold down relatively flat, and have locking mechanisms to keep them in place when they’re in use. But if you have the room, you might prefer the sturdier design of a non-collapsible foot bath.

Many foot baths have features to give you more than a good soak, like bubbles, jets, and massagers. Some will heat up the water for you, and others have helpful elements like remote control, rollers, and pumice stones. These extra features usually come with a higher price, so consider what you will and won’t use if you’re looking to save on a bath.

To choose the best foot baths, I first relied on my own personal experience with these tools, making sure to weed out options I’ve used that have leaked, broken, or just not lived up to the hype. From there, I reached out to three podiatrists located across the country for their feedback on what to look for while shopping for these baths. I also utilized in-house testing by Women’s Health editors for units we got feet into. Each foot bath was evaluated on size, weight, ease of cleaning, and extra features like bubbles and built-in massagers to create the final list. Keeping all of that in mind, these foot baths are worth snapping up to get your soak on.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#4915. The 8 Best Sweater Polos for Men, According to Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Your next best-dressed moment starts from the collar down.

I CONSIDER MYSELF the king of sweaters. I love a good collared shirt, so polos are my go-to in the spring and summer. But once fall and winter roll around, I’m all about sweaters. Even better: a sweater polo. It’s the perfect mashup that combines the collar and button placket of a classic polo with the knit construction of a sweater, giving you a little more texture and warmth than your standard cotton pique. The best sweater polos offer that same versatility. You can dress things up or lean super casual depending on the day and occasion. And not all have to be long-sleeved either.

Short-sleeve versions are also great for tropical vacations or layers under a blazer for the office. Either way, they’re an easy way to switch up your usual sweater rotation from the same ol’ crews or turtlenecks. The Men’s Health fashion crew and I have tried more than 30 over the last three years, paying close attention to fit, fabric, comfort, and versatility to find ones that deserve a spot in your closet.

For the past five years, I’ve tested more than 25 sweater polos, but Uniqlo is easily one of my favorites. It checks all the boxes when it comes to excellent quality, fit, versatility and what really seals the deal—affordability. At just $50, you’re getting a premium knit that could pass for something more expensive. It’s made from a cotton-blend yarn in a structured Milano rib knit that looks and feels more like woven cloth than a stretchy tee. This one feels dense yet comfortable on the skin. I especially love the buttonless, open V-neck collar, which gives some breathing room and makes the whole thing feel a little relaxed.

In terms of fit, it’s roomy through the chest and flexible through the arms without looking oversized. I’ve worn it with jeans and dressed it up with tailored trousers and loafers for dinner. Plus, it comes in plenty of colors that you can rotate between office days and the weekend. After more than three wash cycles, it’s held up nicely. Just be sure to toss it in a mesh laundry bag to keep the knit in good shape.

You don’t have to spend a fortune to get your hands on a good sweater polo. Check out this one from Coofandy. It’s one of the lighter knits that I’ve tested, so it’s wearable through all the seasons. Yes, even in the summertime when the temps stayed around 80 degrees, I didn’t break a sweat at the backyard party. The polyester fabric feels soft against the skin and has a little stretch, which makes it easy to move around in.

It also has a V-neck polo collar to give it that laid-back vibe, while the ribbed cuffs and hem pull everything in for a more fitted, body-contouring look. Styling-wise, you’ve got plenty of options. I’d wear it untucked with jeans or chinos for an everyday fit, but you can also tuck it in pants with a belt for a day on the golf course. This one is not machine washable, so I’d recommend taking a trip to the dry cleaners.

I love mixing different textures in my polo sweater collection, so things don’t start looking too plain. That’s when I add in pieces like Charles Tyrwhitt’s textured knit to give some depth and dimension to my outfit without going overboard with loud patterns or prints. It’s made from 100 percent cotton that’s been garment-washed for a softer, broken-in feel, so I’m not dealing with a stiff, scratchy sweater.

The midweight material is substantial enough to wear on its own during cooler days but breathable enough to layer under a jacket without feeling too bundled up. I’d wear the petrol-blue shade with cream trousers and brown suede loafers for a sharp office look, or pair it with dark denim and boots for dinner. I’ve washed it more than four times and haven’t seen it shrink or pill, but my advice is to let it air dry.

When my brain can’t function in the morning to put an outfit together, I just rely on Abercrombie’s knit. It’s made from 100 percent merino wool, which sounds like it might be a recipe for itchiness, but surprisingly, it feels soft and smooth against the skin. I also dig the classic three-button collar, which gives it a slightly dressier edge than your average crewneck. The fit is also a nice balance, with enough room in the chest and stomach, in case I wolfed down a burger.

Now, I will say that the wool can get a little toasty, especially if you’re moving around a lot. But if your office blasts AC like it’s the middle of Antarctica, you should be just fine. Styling-wise, I’d wear it with straight-leg jeans and sneakers for a casual Friday, or swap in chinos and loafers when I want to look a little more put-together. It only comes in neutrals, which should be easy to pair with anything in your wardrobe.

There’s something about cashmere that makes even the simplest outfit feel a little more luxurious. And if you’re going to invest in a cashmere sweater polo, Quince is a great place to start. This one is made from 100 percent Grade-A Mongolian cashmere, with fine fibers that give the knit an incredibly soft, smooth feel. The 12-gauge construction gives it a refined look without making it feel overly chunky, and the ribbed cuffs and hem help keep its shape. And when I don’t want to wear a dress shirt, this is a great alternative. Throw it on with tailored trousers and loafers for the office, or pair it with dark jeans and boots for dinner.

I’m a big fan of merino wool because it gives you the warmth of a sweater minus all the extra bulk. Banana Republic uses it for this polo, which is a solid option that can transition from the office straight to dinner. No matter how toasty a room gets, I’m never sweating in it. The fabric stays lightweight and breathable, and has enough warmth to come in handy when temperatures drop.

I also like that the fit is pretty straightforward, with slightly dropped shoulders and ribbed cuffs and hem that give it a relaxed but clean finish. The buttoned collar makes it feel a little dressier than your average knit, especially when paired with chinos or tailored trousers. And unlike some wool sweaters that require a trip to the dry cleaner, this one is machine washable, which is always a plus in my book.

Cos gave the classic sweater polo a completely different spin with a buttonless collar that sits closed rather than opening into the usual V-neck. It’s a subtle detail, but one that makes people take a second look at my outfit. This neckline creates a cleaner, more sophisticated look without being overly flashy. I’d pair it with wide-leg trousers and leather loafers for a sharp office fit, or throw it on with relaxed jeans and sneakers for the weekend.

I especially like this kind of silhouette for guys who prefer a minimalist wardrobe but still want something with a little personality. Now, at around $130, it’s definitely on the pricier side, especially when you can find sweater polos for half that amount. But I’d argue you’re paying for a design that’s a refreshing departure from the sweater polos you’re used to seeing, and chances are, you won’t spot five other guys wearing the same thing.

Not every sweater polo needs long sleeves, especially when you can rock one under a blazer. Take this retro-inspired short-sleeve style from Bonobos, which I can wear year-round. My favorite way to style it is under a structured blazer with tailored trousers. It’s dressy enough to skip the traditional button-down shirt, whether you’re heading to an important meeting or a cocktail reception.

It’s also a great piece to pack for vacation, especially if you’re traveling somewhere tropical and need something sharp for a resort dinner. In that case, ditch the blazer and pair it with linen pants or even shorts for a more laid-back look. Plus, the breathable cotton fabric won’t make scorching temps feel even more unbearable. I wore it on a recent trip to Cancún and didn’t break much of a sweat. Depending on your personal style, Bonobos offers this sweater polo in a variety of colors, prints, and textures, so there’s plenty to choose from.

#4913. 12 Best Bar Carts to Elevate Your Entertaining Game (2026)

Bar carts are not just for someone who likes to host a cocktail soirée. In fact, the predecessor of the bar cart was once a Victorian-era tea trolley. Only when the Prohibition hit did these side tables on wheels find their true calling. Many, many iterations later—think: Alvar Aalto’s iconic tea trolley, which has inspired many picks on this list, and USM’s blessedly minimalist spin on the genre—the beauty of this booze trolley remains that it can completely transform a room or give a useless nook some purpose. Though they’ve fallen out of favor in many modern homes, these rolling wonders make an elegant—and functional—home base for all your mixology essentials, from stemware and decanters to liquor bottles and mixers. They also don’t have to be used to haul booze at all, instead doubling as portable storage for crafts, books, beauty or bathroom supplies, and houseplants.

Employed outside, a stylish bar cart can give a dinner party some polish or emulate a poolside butler. Load it up with a pitcher of lemonade and a basket of sunscreen on top, and extra towels on the bottom and you’ll never have to leave your lounge.

Made of solid and veneered walnut with elegant brass details, the Cotu (from the makers of our favorite bar cabinets) is a delightful midcentury-style bar cart that has a distinctive asymmetrical incline on each shelf. Use the wider edge for housing smaller utensils and glasses, while leaving the shallower end for larger bottles that are less likely to topple over the edge.

Birch Lane’s Reinhart cart speaks to farmhouse design, especially in this punchy shade of blue. Turned legs give the overall look a polished appearance, but scalloped paneling on the top shelf and a fun hue ground the piece in something that’s suitable for more playful design aesthetes.

Think of the Wallace Serving Bar Cart as the anti-bar cart. The wooden design resembles a sleek-looking side table thanks to its grounded base, but underneath, a discreet set of wheels gives you the ability to roll the decor piece anywhere a gin and tonic or negroni needs mixing. Its clandestine silhouette also allows it to double as a shelf for non-drink making goods like magazines, coffee table books, or your favorite potted plants.

While this circular cart might lack ample space for large-scale barware, its Art Deco style gives it an Old Hollywood feel. Placed in an area that gets lots of sunshine, the amber tempered glass shelves diffuse a warm glow, layering in some unexpected coziness during cloudless days.

Business & Pleasure Co.’s Al Fresco bar cart is a throwback to a time of leisure under the Parisian sun. While the cart can be used indoors, we can’t imagine a better place for it than on a terrace surrounded by a garden. As if the charming scalloped trim wasn’t enough, the designated umbrella hole nails the summery vibe for poolside mojitos or curbside lemonade stands.

To find that heirloom quality of Victorian design lore, look no further than Greenrow’s Liona bar cart with Barley twist legs to charm you an dyour guests. The two shelves in a chestnut finish offer ample space for glassware and a floral arrangement, should you want to create a whole spread for summer spritzers.

Here’s a piece of decor with lots of Mad Men energy. With its sloped legs and clean-lined silhouette, this cart has enough midcentury-modern charm to appeal to retro design lovers. Two full-size shelves have ample room for old fashioned and martini ingredients, while a mid-tier half shelf can either support a few extra bottles or a stack of your favorite mixology books.

For studio apartment dwellers or homes where square footage is precious, this miniature cart is slim enough to slip into discreet spaces until happy hour rolls around. Made of sturdy beech wood, rounded edges and a light hue soften the beverage cart’s overall look. We think these elements also make it well-suited for adorning Scandi- or Japandi-centric spaces.

Leather accents, exposed wood grain shelves, and an antiqued gold finish bring a polished look and feel to this spacious bar accessory. Two levels with a generous amount of clearance makes it easy to style, whether you’re packing it full of bottles or prefer a more curated decor approach of sculptural glassware.

This sleek, minimalist bar cart will stay with you for many moves. The chrome steel frame defines the iconic silhouette, and you can choose from nine powder-coated steel panels that come in classic black and white, as well as ultra-bold yellow and emerald.

For Bauhaus style on a budget, the Cullin bar cart is more than ready to serve. The angular silhouette resembles less of a cart and more of a full on booze-fueled vehicle, and feels especially cheerful in green or brick red colorways (white and black are also available). With storage for four wine bottles, you can stock multiple kinds of sippers, from sparkling to organic, to please even the snobbiest of guests.

Sturdy and sustainably sourced, this midcentury beauty from West Elm is made in a Fair Trade facility from FSC-certified kiln-dried eucalyptus wood. The soft honey finish of acacia veneer gives this piece accessibility, while the antique brass details add a touch of flair.

#4911. The Best Travel Backpacks for Women in 2026, Tested by Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The right travel backpack helps you master the art of packing light, so you aren’t hauling unnecessary weight to Terminal B. It has enough space for your flight essentials—laptop, passport, water bottle, charging cables—and is comfortable enough to strap on for hours. Whether you need an upgrade to complement your new carry-on, are investing in a pack to carry you through your next adventure, or simply looking for a great Christmas gift, here’s what to consider before you shop.

Below, see the best travel backpacks for women to take on your next adventure.

Topo’s Rover Pack is truly multifunctional, and that’s why we’ve dubbed it our best overall travel backpack. Its thoughtful design, roomy compartments, and casual look make it great for someone who’s always on the move, whether they’re going to the gym, commuting to work, or packing for their next trip.

The backpack has a 20-liter capacity, spread across a large main compartment and a zippered pocket on the front. There’s also a padded internal laptop sleeve, two adjustable water bottle pockets, and more. Plus, it’s made with dual side compression and spacer mesh shoulder straps. While it packs a ton, the bag is midsize enough that it can be used as an everyday bag, too.

The backpack’s main compartment is designed with a drawstring closure that can be cinched closed, and then secured using the two exterior straps with buckle closures. This adds some reassurance that whatever you’ve packed inside won’t spill out, or be at risk of getting stolen on hectic travel days.

We love that this bag comes in more than 15 fun color combinations that will stand out from the rest of the plain backpacks. Bonus points that it’s made from durable recycled nylon.

Most of the best travel backpacks will cost you at least $100—and sometimes more. But the Matein Carry-On Travel Backpack is the exception. This bag is designed with the same features as the other backpacks in this guide for a fraction of the price—under $40. It has more than seven compartments, including a hidden pocket with two ventilation holes that can be used to store shoes up to a size 12 or dirty laundry.

Inside you’ll find a padded neoprene pocket that can fit laptops up to 17 inches. The pocket closes with two zippers that meet, allowing you to add a lock to that particular compartment if you want to deter thieves. One feature we particularly love (in addition to its multiple compartments) is that it’s designed with comfort in mind. The part of the backpack that lies on your lower back when worn is made with extra padding to avoid discomfort, and its straps are padded, too.

A chest strap with a buckle closure would have made this backpack perfect to help distribute some of its weight (40 liters can feel quite heavy to some!), but it does come with a luggage strap you can use to rest it on your carry-on or checked luggage while you’re on your way to your destination.

We also love the hidden pocket in the back to store your most valuable items, like money, your passport, or other documents. To pack the main compartment, you can open the bag up like a clamshell, which makes it easy to store your clothing and other travel essentials in a way that makes the most out of the space you have.

The North Face Borealis is a classic backpack that’s been around for decades—25 years to be exact, and many people who own the cult-favorite bag will tell you they’ve had one for years. The Borealis was originally designed to be used on the trails, but it’s so spacious and easy to organize that it has gained a reputation as a commuter and travel backpack as well.

Assistant social media editor Isabel McMahon says she’s been personally using this bag for years because it’s so comfortable and durable. “The padded back is essential for a long travel day,” she says. McMahon also says the bag’s internal laptop compartment (which fits a computer up to 16 inches) is “next-level,” as it sits a few inches above the bottom of the bag to protect your electronics from accidental drops. The inside also features other small pockets for a phone, documents, and other tiny valuables.

We particularly love that this backpack is designed from a recycled nylon and polyester fabric blend that’s both water-repellent and hard to rip. That’s one of the reasons the bag is so durable—it can truly last decades when cared for. The iconic bungee cord system in the front adds a stylish note that makes this backpack stand apart from other options, but the cords are also functional, too. These can be tightened to hold other essentials, like a water bottle, travel blanket, or jacket.

McMahon’s only complaint about this bag is that there are a lot of straps and clips, which can sometimes get in the way and accidentally snag onto other items, she says. Still, she raves that it makes the perfect bag for a weekend trip at 27 liters.

Another cool feature of this bag is that it’s made with The North Face’s FlexVent system, certified by the American Chiropractic Association. This means the shoulder straps and back panel are designed to contour to the curvature of your spine, so that the bag is easier to hold and there’s less of a chance of you experiencing soreness or fatigue.

Read More: Best Travel Essentials for Women

As denoted by its name, the Triple-Zip Backpack has three main zipper compartments: the main center compartment, the large front pocket, and an external padded laptop pocket that can fit up to a 16-inch laptop. Each pocket is strategically placed, so you have easy access to your laptop, hydration, and any small essentials without having to dig into the main compartment.

Lululemon’s Tech Canvas material features reflective details and is made from recycled polyester, which is water-repellent, making this backpack a great choice for travel. It also has a trolley-compatible sleeve to slip over your luggage while making your way through the airport.

We love the attention to detail built into the thick padded straps—they sit closer together on the back to evenly distribute the load and have an adjustable sternum strap. Plus, load-lifter straps secure the bag to your upper body and the cushy back panel provides lumbar support.

Hikers or outdoor adventurers will enjoy traveling with Cotopaxi’s Allpa 28L Travel Pack. It’s lightweight, made of rip-proof fabric, and easy to clean. Additionally, it’s waterproof, which also makes it a solid choice for those that will face a variety of weather conditions. The Allpa is the backpack I traveled with when I trekked through the Amazon in Ecuador for two days. While there, I regularly had to lay the backpack on the ground for rest and other reasons, so it did get quite dirty. However, I loved that all it took was a good wipe-down to make the bag look brand-new again. I love that it can be easily cleaned using a wet towel, which makes it a solid choice for trips where it can get soiled easily.

Even better? The backpack is made with 100 percent recycled fabric, but it doesn’t skimp on durability. This bag was regularly grazed by tree branches during my hikes or dragged across a floor in my quest to unpack it, and it didn’t experience any rips. It’s made with many of the same features as the other backpacks in this guide—different-sized compartments, a water bottle mesh pocket on the side, and a rollerbag sleeve for resting it on luggage—but it also features four webbing loops along each corner of the bag, which are perfect for attaching gear, like a jacket, clip-on speaker, or a flashlight.

My only gripe with the backpack is that it has so many compartments I lost track of where I put things sometimes. But now that I’ve used it several times, that’s no longer an issue. It’s something first-time users can definitely experience, though.

While the Osprey Fairview is a much pricier buy than the Matein, it’s a lot more supportive (and long-term durable), making it well worth the splurge. Meg Wubbenhorst, a travel expert who has traveled to five continents and over 40 countries, says she regularly used the 40-liter backpack during her 20 months of solo travel, even though she originally thought it looked too small.

“I was pleasantly surprised at the roominess—I sometimes felt like Mary Poppins when unpacking, with ample room for all of my clothes, shoes (no more than 3 pairs!), and various travel accessories,” she says.

From the compression straps on the outside and inside of the bag to the countless mesh compartments and laptop sleeve, this bag makes it easy to get organized, but it’s the backpack’s support features that are impressive. The Osprey bag is made with an adjustable sternum strap that comes with a whistle (particularly useful for adventurers), and a hip belt that helps evenly distribute the bag’s weight to remove strain on your back and shoulders.

It’s also built with Osprey’s proprietary suspension system, which is designed to keep the backpack close to your body, while spreading its load across the entire back panel. This prevents the bag’s weight from pulling you back, so that the bag moves with you as you travel and not against you.

Additionally, whenever you do get tired of carrying this workhorse on your back, you can use either of the convenient carrying handles on its top and left sides. Wubbenhorst also says that she particularly likes that this bag passes most airlines’ carry-on policy, even when it’s stuffed to the gills.

The Kroser Laptop Backpack is a great option for those looking for a backpack for daily use, or those who regularly go on overnight stays. It’s also a great pick for those who prefer to pack their travel backpack with just the essentials—documents, travel blanket, etc. It only holds 37 liters and features multiple pockets for easy organization, including compartments for a laptop, water bottle, pens, and valuables.

Alexandra Dubakova, head of marketing at FreeTour.com, a website for booking local tours, personally likes the Kroser backpack because it’s designed with an aqua blue lining that’s more unique than the usual basic black or brown, and, in her opinion, a lot more functional, too. “That pop of color makes it so much easier to spot my stuff inside the bag,” she says. “I’m always digging around to find things, so having that brighter interior is super handy.” It also features a collapsible steel frame box opening that can give you a bird’s-eye view of what’s in the bag.

On the downside, she doesn’t love that the zippers are bulky and visible, since they make the pockets an easy target for thieves. The bag allows you to secure the two handles with a button once it’s zippered up, though, adding an extra level of security that can provide some extra reassurance that your items will remain safe.

If you’re looking for a backpack that easily fits under your airplane seat, Away’s Active Backpack is a solid choice. It’s also a great option for those that will be taking a backpack on their daily excursions once they arrive at their destination.

First, style-wise the bag is very chic. It’s designed for the outdoors, but it’s stylish enough to take along on your metro adventures without fear it’ll clash with your outfit and be an eyesore in photos. It’s also made from abrasion-resistant material that holds up against the elements—so there’s no problem using this one in rain or snow. While on a trip to Boston, I used this bag during an unexpected flurry of snow, and the bag quickly dried without incident to any of my belongings.

I also found it to be super lightweight. I wore it on the subway to go catch my bus to Boston from New York, and I had no complaints. I packed it with quite a few things—my laptop, some full-sized beauty products, and two days of outfits—and I never felt that the bag was so heavy that I had to put it down to rest.

The Away bag features several compartments, but my favorite is the hidden pocket in the back behind the bag’s straps. I tend to get paranoid that my wallet will get swiped, but storing it back there reassured me that even the savviest thief would likely not find it. Its thoughtful design and lightweight feel make it the perfect everyday bag for longer trips, but it can be used on its own for overnight stays or weekend trips.

What stands out about this Calpak backpack is that it doubles as a duffel bag if you get tired of carrying it on your back. The backpack comes with a removable longer strap you can use to hold the duffel on a shoulder. It also comes with carrying handles—one on the top and one on the side—so you can hold it in whatever orientation feels most comfortable.

Like most of the other backpacks in this guide, it features a ton of pockets, including a zippered water bottle pocket on its left side, a laptop sleeve, an internal mesh pocket, two small zippered compartments in the front of the bag, among several others strategically placed inside the bag. The Terra is designed with a clamshell opening, which makes it relatively easy to pack, and two compression straps in the main compartment designed to hold your contents in place.

Because of its 26-liter capacity, on its own, it’s spacious enough for three to four days of travel, but keep in mind that when it’s packed to the brim, we did find that it was a little tough to get its trolley sleeve over a luggage handle. An extra feature we would have loved to see is a waist strap. It does come with a sternum strap, but a waist strap would make this backpack even more comfortable to carry. This bag does get bonus points for being made from 27 recycled plastic bottles. Sustainability is always a plus.

When shopping for a travel backpack, most brands describe how much it can hold in liters. For longer trips over three days, a larger capacity bag—40 liters or more—is the better choice.

For shorter, weekend-long excursions, you can go for backpacks with a 25- to 30-liter capacity. If you’re using your travel backpack in addition to roller luggage, or as a day bag during your travels, you can go even smaller with 18 to 22 liters. “[Too much] weight can be a bit uncomfortable when traveling around Europe and other places, so I try to stay below 40 liters,” says Tamia Ramsey, a travel expert who has been to over 40 countries and founder of the budget travel blog, Poor in a Private Plane.

Ramsey recommends backpacks with four or more compartments, since they make it easy to organize clothing, electronics, valuables, and other travel essentials. She also finds a pocket in the front particularly useful for storing things you may need on the fly, like a pen.

Other features that can make a travel backpack even more functional are a water bottle holder, a shoe or dirty laundry compartment, and a pocket that isn’t too visible for protecting your wallet, passport, and other valuables from thieves.

Finally, if you want to offset the weight of your bag, you can seek options with sternum and chest straps. These straps typically buckle along the front of your body to redistribute the backpack’s weight and take some of the strain off your back and shoulders.

Travel backpacks can open in a ton of different ways, but some of the most popular options include clamshell, U-shaped, and top-loading designs. A clamshell design opens up like a book, similar to a suitcase. These are easy to pack because they give you a bird’s-eye view of what’s in the bag. Others are top-loading, which means they open up at the top, allowing you to pack from the bottom of the bag up. Finally, backpacks with U-shaped openings are made with a zipper that goes around three sides of the backpack. These provide a wider opening than top-loading backpacks. That allows you to access things quickly without having to lay your bag down on the ground, like you would a backpack with a clamshell opening.

The type of opening you choose depends on your preference, but ones with a clamshell opening are typically the easiest to organize and pack because you get such a great view of what’s inside.

When we first wrote this story in 2025, I considered my own travel experiences, feedback from other Women’s Health editors who travel for work and personal reasons, and spoke with three travel experts who roam the globe on a regular basis. Their intel helped me evaluate the following travel backpacks for women on packability, carry comfort, design, durability, and accessibility.

#4910. The Henley Is Fall’s Most Unexpected Trend—Here’s Why You Need One.

Consider this your sign to rethink the most underrated shirt.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THEY’VE BEEN CROPPING up everywhere. All over my social media feed, featured across men’s runway collections at Fashion Week, seen on Hollywood heartthrobs like Michael B. Jordan, and so forth. If you haven’t figured it out by now, I’m talking about the henley. This once-overlooked wardrobe staple has found new popularity, showing no signs of slowing down as it becomes one of fall’s most surprising menswear trends. And quite frankly, I’m here for it.

The henley hasn’t traditionally been the sexiest shirt in a guy’s wardrobe. For years, it’s been the tee you’d throw on for a lazy Sunday or wear underneath a flannel. But somewhere along the way, the fashion crowd decided it deserved another shot. Its roots go all the way back to 19th-century England, where it started as an undergarment before becoming a go-to for rowers in Henley-on-Thames, hence the name. Who would’ve thought a shirt with such humble beginnings would eventually become a fashion obsession on my Instagram timeline?

Cos Slim Ribbed Cotton Long-Sleeved Henley T-Shirt

Todd Snyder Lightweight Mini Waffle Henley

Cherry Los Angeles Waffle-Knit Cotton-Blend Henley T-Shirt

California Arts Murray Slim Long Sleeve Henley

Here’s what I love about the henley: It does more heavy lifting than your average T-shirt without trying to be anything fancy. You get the simplicity of a crewneck, the button placket of a polo, and just enough texture to make an otherwise basic outfit feel put-together. And while the classic cotton version is still very much in rotation, ribbed, waffle-knit, and thermal styles are giving guys even more ways to wear it. If you need further proof that the henley is having a moment, just take a peek at the runways. For Fall/Winter 2026, Paul Smith sent a model down the runway in a white henley tucked into wide-leg black trousers, while Isabel Marant took a more layered approach, pairing a light blue henley with a navy corduroy jacket.

I’m a firm believer that proportions can make or break an outfit, and the henley is no exception. My favorite way to wear one is with baggy jeans or relaxed trousers. The contrast between a fitted top and roomier bottoms creates a flattering silhouette. And if you’ve spent the past few months putting in work at the gym, a henley is one of the easiest ways to show off those gains without looking like you’re showing off. The closer fit naturally accentuates your chest, shoulders, and biceps, especially when you leave the top button or two undone. Just remember, there’s a fine line between fitted and too tight.

Whether you’re dressing one up with trousers and loafers or keeping things casual with loose jeans and boots, the henley proves that sometimes the most unexpected trends are the pieces we’ve had in our closets all along. And it’s about time this one received its flowers.

#4907. I Have a New Hobby. It’s Kicking My Ass.

The fastest-growing racquet sport in America may also be the cardio workout I’ve been avoiding.

This column first appeared in the Men’s Health email newsletter. The Optimized Man is a biweekly series from our editorial director as he tries out the latest, greatest, and weirdest health and wellness innovations so you don’t have to. Sign up here to get the next one.

I’VE TRIED TO build a life free of shoulds. I’m fine with woulds and coulds and their vague promise of actionability, but when you get into shoulds, you get hung up on stuff like guilt and doubt and all kinds of second-guessing. I really should work out. I really shouldn’t eat that. You think I should try and sleep more? Thanks, man. Good tip.

Shoulds, put plainly, are a problem, and this year I’ve been staring down two different shoulds that won’t quit staring back: I should probably do more cardio, and I should probably get a hobby. I’ve never been much of a cardio guy or a hobby guy, but with evidence tying both to better physical and mental health outcomes, my list of excuses for not doing either is growing short. And I think I’ve found a solution in one of the fastest-growing sports in America.

It’s called padel (pronounced pa-DEL), and you might’ve come across it if you’ve been on vacation lately in Central America or southern Europe (or somewhere really exotic, like Miami). I discovered it last year on a cold winter’s night, and after playing for two hours on an indoor court and emerging sweaty, sore, and exuberant, I can report that it combines everything I like about tennis, racquetball, and squash into one hard-hitting, heavy-breathing sport.

You can go ahead and YouTube the basics, and here’s the gist: You’re playing on a court that’s about three-quarters the area of a tennis court, with high glass walls along the back, some wire fencing on the sides, and a net down the middle. Instead of pickleball’s slow and endless dinking, a padel ball whirs fast off your midsize racquet (also larger and heavier than pickleball’s), and the action requires you to move. Even though it’s a doubles sport (which typically requires less movement than singles, ‘cause there’s two of you), you’re constantly chasing the ball like it’s that little golden bug in quidditch. Sprint, stop, swing, pivot, repeat. (You can also hit the ball against the back wall to launch it in reverse, back over the net, which requires a massive swing.) The first time I played, I showed up wearing sweatpants and a puffer vest over a T-shirt. Within minutes of starting I had sweat through my T-shirt, and by the end of the first set, I had sweat through the seat of my sweatpants. I looked like John Candy in Splash, post-racquetball. What can I say? I’m not a cardio guy.

And there is a lot of cardio here. Back in 2024 we noticed that tennis had started billing itself as “the world’s healthiest sport,” and we asked writer Nick Pachelli to dig into the branding to see how much of it is hype. According to Nick:

Padel isn’t tennis and tennis isn’t padel, but I’ve been playing tennis for almost four decades, and I’ve never had my ass kicked quite as hard as when I played padel.

Then there is the social aspect of it—you’re part of a pair playing another pair, and whether you’re close friends or total strangers with your partner or opponents, at least you’re not bowling alone. Nick found that when longevity researchers study tennis…

Aerobic exercise, social connection and community, some light competition, and a lot of laughs: Could padel be my new hobby? Could it be my main source of cardio? Winter’s coming and the indoor courts are calling, and with visions of John Candy huffing and puffing in my head, I should probably start training.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

Building (and maintaining) upper-body strength as we age is crucial. As well as supporting everyday, functional movements such as lifting, pushing, pulling and reaching, having strong arms can help us get back up again if we were to fall—ultimately meaning we can remain independent for longer.

Sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) can begin to affect us as early as the age of 30. From then, research suggests that muscle mass decreases by approximately 3-8% per decade—with the rate of decline speeding up after 60.

But the good news is that we aren’t powerless in slowing that decline. There’s lots of things we can do, with strength training being one of the most important.

As well as building, well, strength, such training supports other areas of health, too—with one recent study associating two hours of strength work a week with a 22% lower risk of developing major cardiovascular disease and a 44% lower risk of having a heart attack.

#4902. How This Busy Dad Got Leaner and Stronger in 11 Weeks Without Losing Much Weight

Strength coach Gareth Sapstead shares how he helped a busy dad and business owner get leaner, build muscle, and reshape his physique.

Body recomposition is widely viewed as the holy grail of physical transformation: losing body fat while simultaneously adding lean muscle.

It’s also often dismissed as either impossible or reserved exclusively for complete beginners. The logic appears fairly convincing. To lose fat, you need to consume fewer calories than you burn. To build muscle, you need enough energy to construct new tissue. One requires a deficit, the other seemingly demands a surplus.

Pick a lane: bulk first, cut later. Right?

Strength and physique coach Gareth Sapstead disagrees. In a detailed breakdown published on his website, Sapstead explains how he helped father and business owner Mark Schadenberg transform his physique ahead of a Men’s Health Netherlands photoshoot—losing fat, adding visible muscle and finishing just 4 pounds lighter after 11 weeks.

The scales barely budged, but his body changed dramatically.

“The fitness industry has been telling you to pick one for decades,” says Sapstead. “Bulk first, cut later. Build the muscle, then reveal it.”

Sapstead accepts that fat loss requires an energy deficit, while building muscle requires energy. However, he says the apparent contradiction comes from treating your body like a single energy account.

“Fat tissue and muscle tissue operate through different pathways,” he explains. “You can be breaking down stored fat for fuel while simultaneously building muscle protein—as long as the conditions for muscle protein synthesis are met.”

Those conditions are relatively straightforward: enough protein and a sufficiently challenging resistance-training stimulus.

Sapstead points towards research examining simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain. According to Sapstead, the phenomenon appeared consistently across the research and wasn’t simply a beginner-only fluke.

He also references studies in which participants consumed between 400 and 800 additional calories each day, all from protein.

By conventional logic, those extra calories should have resulted in weight gain. Instead, Sapstead says the participants either maintained their weight or lost fat while gaining or preserving muscle.

“Body recomposition is real,” he concludes. “It’s well-supported, and for the right person in the right circumstances, it happens faster than most expect.”

Schadenberg had just 11 weeks to prepare for his photoshoot. He was running a business and raising a family—a familiar combination for many of us—that had gradually pushed training, nutrition, and recovery down his list of priorities.

“He’d let his training slip,” says Sapstead. “Not from a lack of drive, but through the entirely predictable reality of running a business and raising a family.”

His sleep was suffering, his diet lacked structure and he had no consistent exercise routine. Like many men in their late 30s and 40s, Sapstead says, he was also “chronically undereating protein.”

That might not sound like an ideal starting point, but it gave Schadenberg several powerful variables to improve almost immediately.

“Every one of those factors is a recomposition accelerant,” says Sapstead.

Returning to resistance training after a significant lay-off can produce a response closer to that of a beginner. The stimulus feels novel again, adaptations arrive quickly and previously built muscle may return faster than it took to develop in the first place.

Combine that with more protein, better recovery and structured training, and you can create the conditions to rebuild muscle while using stored body fat to help cover the energy costs.

“The body has been starved of the right inputs,” says Sapstead. “Give it protein, training and adequate recovery, and it responds.”

After 11 weeks, Schadenberg was only 4 pounds lighter. But his before-and-after photographs showed considerably more muscle and significantly less body fat.

“Fat came off. Muscle went on. Bodyweight barely moved,” says Sapstead.

Sapstead says recomposition is particularly well suited to anyone who has been away from consistent strength training, is carrying more body fat than they would like, habitually eats too little protein or has allowed sleep and recovery to deteriorate.

For experienced lifters who have trained intelligently, eaten well, and slept properly for years, the process is likely to be slower. There’s simply less low-hanging fruit.

For returning lifters, however, they're in a prime position for a recomp.

This isn’t the time for an aggressive diet or an uncontrolled bulk. Sapstead recommends eating around your maintenance calories or slightly above them, with approximately 200 to 300 additional calories coming predominantly from protein.

The aim is to provide enough energy to support training and muscle growth without creating a large surplus that encourages unnecessary fat gain.

Sapstead sets protein at around one gram per pound of bodyweight as a starting point, although higher intakes may also be appropriate.

Protein provides the raw materials required to repair and construct muscle tissue. It is also highly satiating, making it easier to control your overall food intake without constantly feeling hungry.

Perform three to four structured resistance-training sessions each week, with a focus on progressive overload.

Your body needs a reason to preserve and build muscle. That means gradually adding weight, completing more reps, improving your range of motion or producing better-quality work—not simply getting hot and tired doing random circuits, or going through the motions with zero intensity.

When fat is coming off while muscle is being added, your bodyweight may barely change. That doesn’t mean the approach has stopped working. It may mean it’s working exactly as intended.

“The scale would have told him nothing was happening,” Sapstead says of Schadenberg’s transformation. “The photos would have told him everything.”

Take progress pictures every two to three weeks, track your gym performance and pay attention to how your clothes fit. If your waist is shrinking, your strength is improving and you look more muscular, a stable bodyweight isn’t failure—it’s the holy grail of body recomp in action.

With almost 18 years in the health and fitness space as a personal trainer, nutritionist, breath coach and writer, Andrew has spent nearly half of his life exploring how to help people improve their bodies and minds.

As our fitness editor he prides himself on keeping Men’s Health at the forefront of reliable, relatable and credible fitness information, whether that’s through writing and testing thousands of workouts each year, taking deep dives into the science behind muscle building and fat loss or exploring the psychology of performance and recovery.

Whilst constantly updating his knowledge base with seminars and courses, Andrew is a lover of the practical as much as the theory and regularly puts his training to the test tackling everything from Crossfit and strongman competitions, to ultra marathons, to multiple 24 hour workout stints and (extremely unofficial) world record attempts.
